passage:
"Akka, can I ask you something without you laughing?" Sudha hugged a cushion.
"Promise," Lavanya said, closing her laptop.
"There's a boy in my tuition class. When he talks to me my face goes hot and my stomach flips. I can't stop thinking about him. Is that weird?"
"Not weird at all. Crushes and those fluttery feelings are a normal part of growing up."
"Some girls say I should message him first and not tell Amma. I'm scared Amma will think I'm bad."
"Liking someone doesn't make you bad. You don't have to rush into anything, and you never have to do anything you're not ready for. Secrets make things feel heavier. You can always talk to me, and Amma is kinder about this than you think."
"So what do I do?"
"Just talk to him in class like anyone else, and see how it feels."
Sudha let out a long breath. "Okay. That feels better."

qa.q: Where is the boy Sudha likes?
qa.a: In her tuition class.

qa.q: What was Sudha afraid of?
qa.a: She was afraid of being judged, worried that Amma would think she was bad for having a crush.

qa.q: What guidance from Lavanya helps Sudha make careful choices?
qa.a: That crushes are normal, there is no need to rush, and talking openly with a trusted person is better than keeping secrets.

qa.q: How does Lavanya treat Sudha's question?
qa.a: She takes it seriously, closing her laptop and keeping her promise not to laugh, and treats the feelings as normal.

grounding: Shows a teenager with a sudden crush and confusing feelings, afraid of judgment, and a trusted older sister giving calm, respectful guidance.

passage:
Last year I fell hard for Ritu from the chemistry lab. I replayed every word she said, and when she walked past, my whole body buzzed in a way that honestly scared me. I didn't understand half of what I felt, and I was sure my parents would think I was being stupid. Some friends said, "Just sneak out to the mall with her. Nobody has to know." I almost did. Instead I asked my Mama, who's easy to talk to, on a long walk. He didn't laugh. He said these feelings are normal at my age, that bodies react in confusing ways, and that a careful choice is one you'd be fine with your family knowing about. He said respect goes both ways, and Ritu gets to decide what she wants too. In the end I asked her to the science fair, openly. We're friends now, and that feels right.
Kamal

qa.q: Where did Kamal ask Ritu to go in the end?
qa.a: To the science fair.

qa.q: How did Kamal feel about the new feelings at first?
qa.a: Kamal felt confused and a bit scared, and feared the parents would think it stupid.

qa.q: What was the careful choice, and why?
qa.a: Talking to Mama and then asking Ritu openly instead of sneaking out, because a choice you would be fine with family knowing about is safer and more respectful.

qa.q: How might Ritu have felt being asked openly rather than to sneak out?
qa.a: She could decide freely, without secrecy or pressure, which respects what she wants.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager with a sudden crush and confusing sensations choosing a trusted adult's factual guidance over a secretive plan.

passage: In Lagos, every time Omar from the debate team smiled at her across the library, Nkechi's face went hot and her stomach did a strange flip. She wrote his name in the margin of her notebook, then scribbled over it until the page tore. When he asked if she wanted to go to the cinema, just the two of them, on Saturday, she said "Maybe" and fled. That night she couldn't sleep, torn between excitement and fear. What would her mother say? What would the girls at church say? Should she just go and not tell anyone? In the morning she sat on the edge of Aunty Ifeoma's bed instead. Aunty listened without laughing. "Crushes are normal, and so are the fizzy feelings. What matters is that you choose carefully and don't do things in secret." They agreed Nkechi would invite Omar on the group trip to the beach with her cousins, and see how it felt.

qa.q: What did Nkechi write in her notebook margin?
qa.a: Omar's name.

qa.q: What was Nkechi feeling that kept her awake that night?
qa.a: She felt torn between excitement and fear, worried what her mother and the girls at church would think.

qa.q: Why was talking to Aunty Ifeoma wiser than going in secret?
qa.a: A trusted adult gave calm, factual reassurance and helped Nkechi choose a careful, open plan instead of a secretive one.

qa.q: How might Omar feel when Nkechi says "Maybe" and runs?
qa.a: Omar might feel confused or hopeful, unsure whether she likes him.

grounding: Shows a teenager with a first crush, fizzy feelings and fear of judgment turning to a trusted adult and choosing an open, careful plan.

passage: The anonymous question box outside the counsellor's room at a school in Bhopal held a new note on Monday: "Is it normal to think about someone all the time and feel your heart race when they walk in? Is it wrong if they're a girl?" On Wednesday Reena lingered after health class, pretending to tie her shoe. Nazia Ma'am, the counsellor, noticed and didn't rush her. "Some questions are easier in private," she said, and closed the door. Reena went red. "It was mine." Nazia nodded calmly. "Crushes and racing-heart feelings are a normal part of growing up, whoever they're for. Feelings aren't wrong. What matters is being kind, respectful and careful about what you do." Reena let out a long breath. They talked about taking things slowly and not rushing into anything, and Nazia said her door was open whenever Reena needed it.

qa.q: Where was the anonymous question box?
qa.a: Outside the counsellor's room at a school in Bhopal.

qa.q: What was Reena feeling when she lingered after class?
qa.a: She felt nervous and ashamed, afraid her feelings were wrong and worried about being judged.

qa.q: What made Nazia Ma'am a trusted adult here?
qa.a: She offered privacy, answered calmly and factually without judging, and focused on kind, careful choices.

qa.q: How might Nazia see Reena's question?
qa.a: As a normal, brave question about growing up that deserves a respectful, private answer.

grounding: Shows a teenager confused by a crush and afraid of judgment, and a counsellor giving respectful, factual guidance toward careful choices.

passage:
Dear Ramesh Mama,
You said I could write to you about anything, so here goes.
There's a boy in my class, Tenzin. When he laughs, my face goes hot and I forget what I was saying. I think about him at night, and I feel happy and scared and a bit stupid, all at the same time. Some girls say I should just go to his house when his parents are out, like they do. That made my stomach twist, and not in a good way.
I don't want to do anything secret. But I also don't want Amma to laugh at me or be angry. Is what I'm feeling normal? And how do I talk to her about it?
Your confused niece,
Pema

qa.q: What happens to Pema when Tenzin laughs?
qa.a: Pema's face goes hot and she forgets what she was saying.

qa.q: What mix of feelings is Pema describing?
qa.a: Pema feels happy, scared and a bit stupid all at once, and uneasy about the girls' suggestion.

qa.q: Why is writing to Ramesh Mama a careful choice?
qa.a: It brings in a trusted adult for respectful guidance and help talking to Amma, instead of making secretive decisions under pressure.

qa.q: How might Ramesh Mama feel reading the letter?
qa.a: He may feel touched to be trusted and keen to reassure her that the feelings are normal and help her talk to Amma.

grounding: Shows a teenager with a new crush, confusing feelings and peer pressure turning to a trusted adult rather than making a secretive choice.

passage: Ayesha, promise you won't laugh. Okay. So Leela, the girl who said crushes are silly, has a crush. On Rehaan from debate club. Whenever he walks past, my face goes hot, my stomach flips and I forget how to talk. Last week I went red just because he borrowed my pen. It's so confusing. My body does things I didn't ask for, and I kept thinking something was wrong with me, or that Mummy would be furious. Then an older boy from tuition started messaging me to meet him secretly, and I almost said yes just to feel grown-up. Instead I told my Masi that same evening. She didn't scold. She said these feelings are normal, that I get to go slow, and that anyone who wants secrets from adults isn't safe. I blocked that boy that night. Rehaan can stay a nice feeling for now.

qa.q: What happens when Rehaan walks past Leela?
qa.a: Her face goes hot, her stomach flips, and she forgets how to talk.

qa.q: What was Leela worried about?
qa.a: She was anxious that something was wrong with her and scared that Mummy would be furious.

qa.q: What did Masi help Leela decide?
qa.a: That the feelings are normal, she can go slow, and anyone wanting secrets from adults isn't safe, so Leela blocked the older boy.

qa.q: How might Ayesha feel hearing Leela's story?
qa.a: Ayesha may feel trusted, and relieved that Leela talked to Masi instead of meeting the older boy.

grounding: A teenager with a first crush and confusing feelings turns to a trusted adult and chooses care over secrecy.
